editorial.headline: Wooden Construction Materials: Nationally Open, Blocked for PMA in Bali
editorial.standfirst: Wholesale wooden construction materials are nationally open to 100% foreign ownership, but Bali’s permanent PMA moratorium blocks registration for this activity.
editorial.body:
Wooden construction materials, in this activity, are defined as a wholesale subject with a deliberately broad product boundary. The scope includes boards, scantling, roof battens, trim boards, telephone and electricity poles, sleeper beams, door and window frames, and door and window leaves. It also names wood tiles, wooden shingles, plywood—including tripleks, interior plywood and plywood for concrete formwork—together with teak wood, particle board, chip board and wood veneers. The organising idea is not wood in the abstract, but wholesale trade in the specifically listed materials and components for construction. Sheet goods, joinery pieces, finishing stock and heavier construction elements are all expressly present in that definition.

The registration frame is equally broad across business scale. The record admits Micro, Small, Medium and Large businesses (Mikro, Kecil, Menengah and Besar), so an operator registering this activity can fall at any of those listed scales. That detail deserves a careful reading: the activity’s listed scale eligibility is national information, while Bali’s outcome turns on the recorded risk treatment of the Besar scale. The two points sit in the same record but answer different questions—who may register nationally at the stated scale, and whether a PMA registration can be made in Bali.

Nationally, the position is open. The PMA status is TERBUKA, with a national foreign-ownership ceiling of 100%, citing Perpres 10/2021 and 49/2021. In practical terms, the record allows a fully foreign-owned PMA registration for this activity at national level. It is not presented as a minority-cap category or as closed in the national field: the ceiling stated for this code is 100%. That is the national baseline. It does not, however, decide Bali’s distinct registration outcome.

In Bali, the answer is unambiguous: a PMA business cannot register this activity today. The Bali status is BLOCCATO_CLASSE_RISCHIO. Its recorded reason is that OSS places the Besar-scale risk at Low or Medium-Low across every scope, bringing the activity within Bali’s permanent, island-wide PMA moratorium. The block is recorded as applying from May 2026. The contrast is therefore not a reduced foreign-ownership percentage in Bali; it is a block on PMA registration. A national ceiling of 100% remains the national position, but it does not displace Bali’s block for this activity.
